title: Globalization and Today
bigQuestion: In a world where money, goods, people, diseases and ideas cross borders in hours, who decides anything, and how can a citizen tell what is true?

story.title: Three Journeys Around One World
story.kicker: A ship the length of four football fields, a phone in your pocket and the shirt on your back each tell the same story: nothing you own comes from one place anymore.
paragraphs: Start with the ship. It leaves the port of Shanghai carrying about twenty thousand steel boxes, each the size of a truck trailer. Nobody on board knows what is in most of them. That is the point. Before the 1960s, dockworkers loaded ships by hand, sack by sack and crate by crate, and a ship could sit in port for a week. In 1956 an American trucking owner named Malcom McLean put fifty-eight truck bodies on a tanker and sailed them from New Jersey to Texas. The standard *container* was born. A crane can now move a box from ship to train to truck in minutes, and the cost of shipping a T-shirt across the Pacific fell to a few cents. That box, more than any treaty, built the world economy you live in.

Now the phone. Its screen glass may come from Kentucky. The processor was designed in California and made in Taiwan. The memory chips came from South Korea, the camera lens from Japan, the battery from China. The cobalt in that battery was probably dug in Congo, some of it by people, including children, working in dangerous pits. The whole thing was assembled in a Chinese factory city where hundreds of thousands of workers live in dormitories, and shipped in a container. It runs software written by people in a dozen countries. No single person on Earth knows how to make the phone from scratch.

Finally the shirt. The cotton may have grown in Texas or in India. It was spun into thread and woven into cloth, perhaps in China, and cut and sewn in Bangladesh, where a garment worker might earn a few dollars a day. In April 2013 a factory building called Rana Plaza collapsed near Dhaka, killing more than eleven hundred workers who had been ordered back inside after cracks appeared in the walls. Many of them were sewing clothes for Western brands. The shirt came to Illinois through a warehouse near Joliet, one of the largest inland freight hubs in North America, and reached you by truck.

Each journey shows the same pattern. Work is split into pieces and sent wherever it can be done cheapest. Goods, money and information move almost freely; people, mostly, do not. Prices fall, and more people than ever before can afford phones and shirts. At the same time, a factory closes in Rockford or Decatur, a worker in Bangladesh dies under a concrete slab, and a child in Congo digs cobalt. The word for all of this is *globalization*, and this chapter is about the world it has made: richer and more connected than any before, and full of problems that no one country can solve alone.
story.think: Pick one object you are wearing or carrying. List every country you think touched it. Who gained from each step, and who might have paid?

lessons.title: Wired Together
lessons.mainIdea: In one generation the internet went from a scientists' tool to the nervous system of the world, changing how people work, learn, shop and argue.
reading: In 1969 a computer at the University of California sent the first message over a network built for the American defense department. The message was supposed to be the word login. The system crashed after two letters. For twenty years the network, called ARPANET and then the Internet, connected mainly universities and research labs. Then in 1989 a British scientist named Tim Berners-Lee, working at a physics lab in Switzerland, proposed a way to link documents on any computer to documents on any other. He called it the World Wide Web and gave it away free. By 1995 about sixteen million people were online. By 2005 about a billion. Today it is more than five billion, most of them through a phone.

The change was not only in speed. The internet erased distance for information. A doctor in Chicago can read a study published in Tokyo an hour after it appears. A student in Kenya can take a free course from a university in Massachusetts. A factory in Vietnam receives its design files from Germany overnight. Companies could now split work across continents and coordinate it in real time, which made the global supply chains in this chapter's opening story possible. Whole industries appeared, from search engines to ride-hailing, and others such as travel agencies and record stores nearly vanished.

The *smartphone*, introduced in its modern form in 2007, put all of this in a pocket. For billions of people in Africa and Asia, a phone was their first camera, bank account, newspaper and map. Farmers check crop prices before walking to market. Migrants send money home by text. Protesters in Tunisia and Egypt in 2011 organized on social media faster than governments could react. At the same time, governments learned to use the same tools. China built a system that blocks foreign websites and tracks its citizens online. Companies in the United States built businesses on collecting what users click, watch and buy.

The internet is a *network*, a web with no center, and that shape explains both its strength and its danger. No government owns it. Anyone can publish. That freed voices that had never been heard and also freed liars, scammers and mobs. The same tools that let a village clinic order medicine let a criminal in one country empty a bank account in another. The last section of this chapter returns to the question that the internet made urgent for every citizen: with everyone able to speak, how do you know whom to believe?

words.d: the worldwide network of connected computer networks
a mobile phone that is also a computer connected to the internet
a system of connected points with no single center, like a web
the linked steps, often in many countries, by which a product is designed, made and delivered

look.title: People Using the Internet
look.prompt: About how many times did the number of users grow between 1995 and 2005? What happened after 2007 that helps explain the later rows?

check.q: What did Tim Berners-Lee contribute in 1989?
choices: He built the first computer
He proposed the World Wide Web, a way to link documents on any computer, and gave it away free
He invented the smartphone
He founded the first search engine
check.why: The Web turned a research network into something anyone could publish on and read, and its free release let it spread everywhere.

check.q: How did the internet make global supply chains possible?
choices: It made ships faster
It replaced factories with computers
Companies could split work across continents and coordinate it in real time
It ended the need for shipping
check.why: Instant sharing of designs and orders let companies place each step of production wherever it was cheapest.

check.q: Why does the reading say the internet's shape explains both its strength and its danger?
choices: A web with no center lets anyone publish, which frees new voices and also frees liars and criminals
It is owned by one government that controls everything
It has a center that can be switched off
It works only in rich countries
check.why: No owner and no gatekeeper means freedom for everyone, including those who mean harm.

lessons.title: Trade Without Borders
lessons.mainIdea: Falling shipping costs and new trade agreements tied the world's economies together, creating enormous wealth and sharp losers at the same time.
reading: In 1994 the United States, Canada and Mexico joined in the North American Free Trade Agreement, removing most tariffs among them. In 1995 the *World Trade Organization* was founded to write and enforce trade rules for the whole world; it now has more than one hundred and sixty members. Together with the container ship and the internet, these rules made it cheap and safe to build a product across many countries. World trade grew far faster than the world economy. A company in Peoria could now sell tractors in Brazil and buy parts from Poland, and a shopper in Springfield could buy a television for a fraction of what it had cost her parents.

The gains were real and huge. Between 1990 and 2019 the share of the world's people living in extreme poverty, on less than about two dollars a day, fell from roughly one in three to under one in ten. Most of that change came in Asia, where factories making goods for export pulled hundreds of millions off farms and into cities. Life expectancy rose, child deaths fell, and more girls went to school than at any time in history. Economists who disagree about almost everything mostly agree that open trade made the world as a whole richer.

But the world as a whole is not a person. The gains and losses landed on different people. In the American Midwest, factories that had paid good wages to workers without a college degree closed as production moved to Mexico or China. Towns like Galesburg, Illinois, where a large appliance plant shut in 2004 and moved to Mexico, lost their largest employer and never fully recovered. Economists found that regions hit by import competition saw lasting drops in jobs and wages and rises in disability and family breakdown. The people who gained from cheaper goods were spread across the country; the people who lost were concentrated in specific places, and they noticed.

By the 2010s a backlash was growing on both the political left and right. Critics argued that trade deals served corporations, that workers in poor countries were exploited, and that a country that made nothing was not safe. Defenders replied that closing borders would raise prices, cost more jobs than it saved, and hurt the poorest countries most. Both sides had evidence. In 2018 the United States began imposing new tariffs on China and China answered in kind, and the COVID pandemic of 2020 showed how fragile long supply chains could be when a single factory closed. The question of how open the world's economy should be is not settled, and your generation will help decide it.

words.d: the growing connection of the world's economies and cultures through trade, travel, money and information
the international body founded in 1995 that sets and enforces rules for trade among its members
trade between countries with few or no tariffs or other barriers
living on less than about two dollars a day, the World Bank's line for the poorest

look.title: Share of the World in Extreme Poverty
look.prompt: The world's population also grew a great deal in these years. Does that make the fall in the percentage more impressive or less? Where did most of the change happen, and why?

check.q: What happened to the share of the world's people in extreme poverty between 1990 and 2019?
choices: It rose
It stayed the same
It fell from roughly one in three to under one in ten
It fell only in Europe
check.why: Export-driven growth, mostly in Asia, pulled hundreds of millions out of extreme poverty.

check.q: Why did the losers from trade notice their losses more than the winners noticed their gains?
choices: Losers were concentrated in specific towns while gains from cheaper goods were spread thinly across everyone
There were no gains at all
Winners were forced to pay the losers
The news reported only bad stories
check.why: A closed factory devastates one town, while a slightly cheaper television is spread over millions of shoppers.

check.q: What did the 2020 pandemic reveal about long supply chains?
choices: They were unbreakable
They could be fragile, since one closed factory could halt production far away
They only existed in Asia
They had no effect on prices
check.why: The reading notes that a single factory closure could stop supply chains that stretched across many countries.

lessons.title: China Rises
lessons.mainIdea: After 1978 China combined one-party rule with market reforms and became the world's factory and its second-largest economy, changing the balance of power.
reading: When Mao died in 1976, China was poor. Most of its people were peasants, and a bad harvest still meant hunger. Its new leader, Deng Xiaoping, had been purged twice under Mao and had no interest in repeating his experiments. In 1978 he began to let farmers sell what they grew above a quota, and harvests jumped. He opened special economic zones on the coast, starting with a fishing town called Shenzhen, where foreign companies could build factories with cheap labor and low taxes. Deng's slogan was that it did not matter whether a cat was black or white as long as it caught mice. Shenzhen is now a city of more than twelve million.

The results were the fastest sustained growth any large country has recorded. For three decades China's economy grew close to ten percent a year, doubling roughly every seven years. It joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, and its exports flooded the world. By 2010 it had passed Japan to become the second-largest economy on Earth. About eight hundred million Chinese people escaped extreme poverty, by the World Bank's count, the largest such change in history. Cities of skyscrapers rose where rice fields had been. China built more high-speed rail in fifteen years than the rest of the world combined.

Growth did not bring democracy. The Communist Party kept its monopoly on power, as it had shown at Tiananmen in 1989. It censors the internet, jails critics, and has held perhaps a million Uyghur Muslims in camps in the western region of Xinjiang, which the government calls vocational training and human rights groups and several governments call mass detention. The party's bargain with its people was prosperity in exchange for obedience. For many years, with incomes rising, most accepted it. Whether the bargain holds as growth slows and the population ages is one of the great open questions of your lifetime.

China's rise changed the world's map of power. It is the largest trading partner of most countries on Earth, including many in Africa and Latin America, where it builds ports, railroads and stadiums in exchange for resources and influence. It has built a large navy and claims most of the South China Sea. The United States, which welcomed China into the world economy hoping trade would make it more open, now treats it as its chief rival. Whether the two will compete, cooperate or collide is a question American and Chinese students will inherit. Illinois soybeans, Boeing planes and Caterpillar machines, all sold to China, are one measure of what is at stake.

words.d: an area where a government allows foreign investment and market rules it does not allow elsewhere
changes that let prices, profit and private business replace government planning
government control over what people may publish, read or see
a country in which a single political party holds all power and no opposition is allowed

look.title: Two Views of Shenzhen
look.text: A woman who left a mountain village at eighteen to sew phone cases in Shenzhen now owns an apartment and sends her daughter to college; she thinks the party gave her a life her mother never dreamed of. A lawyer who tried to help factory workers claim unpaid wages was arrested and has not been seen in a year.
look.prompt: Both stories are typical of modern China. How would each person answer the question of whether the bargain of prosperity for obedience is a fair one?

check.q: What did Deng Xiaoping's cat slogan mean?
choices: That only communist methods were acceptable
That results mattered more than whether a method was capitalist or socialist
That China should keep out foreign companies
That farmers should not own cats
check.why: Deng was willing to use market tools if they made China richer, which is why he opened zones like Shenzhen.

check.q: Which statement about China's growth after 1978 is correct?
choices: It brought multi-party democracy
It ended because of the Tiananmen protests
It lifted about eight hundred million people out of extreme poverty while the party kept a monopoly on power
It happened mainly through farming
check.why: China's growth was the largest reduction in poverty in history, but political control did not loosen.

check.q: Why did the United States welcome China into the world economy, according to the reading?
choices: To sell it nuclear weapons
Because the Soviet Union demanded it
To make Chinese goods more expensive
In the hope that trade would make China more open
check.why: American leaders expected that prosperity and trade would lead to a more open China, a hope that has not been fulfilled.

lessons.title: Europe Unites, Mostly
lessons.mainIdea: Countries that had fought two world wars built a union with open borders and a shared currency, and then discovered how hard it is to share decisions.
reading: In 1951, six years after the war, France, West Germany, Italy and three small neighbors agreed to run their coal and steel industries jointly. The idea, pushed by the French planner Jean Monnet, was that countries whose steel was shared could not build tanks to fight each other. The community grew into a common market with no tariffs among its members. In 1992 the members signed a treaty at Maastricht creating the *European Union*, with a shared citizenship, plans for a single currency and a promise to act together on foreign policy. Border checks between most members disappeared. A German could drive to Spain without showing a passport.

In 2002 twelve countries replaced their francs, marks and lire with the *euro*, the first time major nations had given up their own money for a shared one. In 2004 ten more countries, most of them former Soviet satellites, joined the Union, and Poland, Hungary and the Baltic states that had escaped the iron curtain in 1989 became full members of the West. By the 2010s the EU had twenty-eight members and about five hundred million people, the largest economy in the world by some measures, with a parliament, a court and rules that governed everything from phone charges to the shape of bananas.

Then the strains showed. A shared currency meant Greece and Germany had the same money but very different economies, and when Greece could not pay its debts after 2009, Germans resented paying to rescue it while Greeks resented the cuts demanded in return. When more than a million refugees arrived in 2015, mostly from the Syrian war, countries argued bitterly over who should take them. Many citizens felt that decisions were being made in Brussels by people they had never voted for. In June 2016 British voters chose, by fifty-two to forty-eight percent, to leave. Britain left in January 2020, the first member ever to do so.

The EU today has twenty-seven members and a hard question at its center. Its founders believed that sharing *sovereignty*, a country's right to make its own decisions, was the price of peace and prosperity. Its critics believe that a democracy has to be small enough for citizens to control it. Russia's full invasion of Ukraine in 2022 pushed the members closer together again, and Ukraine itself asked to join. The Union has kept its members from fighting one another for seventy years, which no earlier arrangement in Europe ever managed. Whether it can also make decisions its citizens accept is still being tested.

words.d: the political and economic union of European countries created by the Maastricht Treaty of 1992
the shared currency used by most EU members since 2002
a country's right to govern itself and make its own laws
a group of countries that trade among themselves without tariffs

look.title: The Steel Bargain
look.text: In 1951 France and West Germany, enemies in three wars over eighty years, put their coal and steel under one authority. A French steelworker in Lorraine and a German steelworker in the Ruhr now answered to the same rules and shipped to the same customers.
look.prompt: Why would sharing an industry make war less likely? What does a country give up when it makes a deal like this, and what has Europe gotten in return?

check.q: What was the original purpose of pooling coal and steel in 1951?
choices: To make steel cheaper for the United States
To make it impossible for France and Germany to rearm against each other
To compete with the Soviet Union's steel
To create a common currency
check.why: Shared control of the materials of war was meant to make another Franco-German war unthinkable.

check.q: Which problem did the shared euro create after 2009?
choices: Nobody would accept the new money
Prices rose in every country at once
Countries with very different economies shared one currency, and rescuing Greece caused resentment on both sides
The euro made Britain leave immediately
check.why: A single currency without a single economy meant Germany paid to rescue Greece while Greece accepted painful cuts.

check.q: What is the central disagreement about the EU described in the reading?
choices: Whether Europe should have any trade at all
Whether the euro should be replaced by the dollar
Whether Britain should rejoin NATO
Whether sharing sovereignty is the price of peace or a loss of democratic control
check.why: Supporters see pooled decision-making as the key to peace; critics say citizens cannot control a government so distant.

lessons.title: September 11 and the Wars After
lessons.mainIdea: The attacks of September 11, 2001, led the United States into two long wars whose costs and results are still debated.
reading: On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen men hijacked four airliners. They flew two into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, one into the Pentagon near Washington, and the fourth, after passengers fought back, crashed in a Pennsylvania field. Nearly three thousand people were killed, more than in any attack on American soil. The hijackers belonged to al-Qaeda, a network led by Osama bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi who had fought the Soviets in Afghanistan and now called for war against the United States. He was sheltered by the Taliban, the extremist group ruling most of Afghanistan.

*Terrorism* means using violence against civilians to spread fear for a political goal. It is a tactic, not a country, and that made the response hard to define. In October 2001 the United States and its allies invaded Afghanistan, drove out the Taliban within weeks, and began trying to build a new government. In March 2003 the United States invaded Iraq, arguing that its dictator, Saddam Hussein, had weapons of mass destruction and ties to terrorists. No such weapons were found, and the claimed ties proved false. Saddam was overthrown, but Iraq fell into years of civil war among religious and ethnic groups, in which American troops were caught.

The wars lasted far longer than anyone planned. The Iraq war killed about forty-five hundred American troops and an estimated hundreds of thousands of Iraqis. The chaos in Iraq and Syria produced the Islamic State, or ISIS, which seized a territory the size of Britain in 2014 and was broken by 2019. In Afghanistan the Taliban never went away, and after twenty years, in August 2021, the last American troops left and the Taliban retook the country within days. About twenty-four hundred Americans and far larger numbers of Afghans had died there. Illinois National Guard units served in both wars, and the names of the state's dead are recorded in Springfield.

The wars changed life at home. A new Department of Homeland Security was created. Airport searches, which barely existed before 2001, became routine. Laws expanded the government's power to watch communications, and prisoners were held for years without trial at a naval base in Cuba. Americans argued, and still argue, about the balance between safety and freedom, and about whether the wars made the country safer or created new enemies. Historians will judge with more evidence than we have. What is already clear is that a single morning redirected two decades of American power and cost trillions of dollars.

words.d: the use of violence against civilians to create fear and force a political change
the network led by Osama bin Laden that carried out the September 11 attacks
the extremist movement that ruled Afghanistan before 2001 and again after 2021
nuclear, chemical or biological weapons able to kill large numbers of people

look.title: Two Arguments in 2003
look.text: One advisor says: Saddam is a brutal dictator, the intelligence reports say he is building terrible weapons, and after September 11 we cannot wait for proof. Another says: the intelligence is thin, invading a country of twenty-five million will unleash forces we cannot control, and we will be blamed for whatever follows.
look.prompt: Knowing what happened next, which advisor was right, and about what? How should leaders decide when the evidence is uncertain and the cost of being wrong is high either way?

check.q: Why did the United States invade Afghanistan in October 2001?
choices: Afghanistan had attacked American ships
The Taliban government sheltered al-Qaeda, which carried out the September 11 attacks
Afghanistan had weapons of mass destruction
The Soviet Union asked for help
check.why: Bin Laden's network was based in Afghanistan under Taliban protection, and the invasion aimed to destroy it.

check.q: What happened to the main justification for the 2003 invasion of Iraq?
choices: The weapons were found and destroyed
Iraq admitted the weapons existed
No weapons of mass destruction were found, and the claimed terrorist ties proved false
The United Nations confirmed the weapons
check.why: The reading states that no such weapons were found and the ties to terrorists were not real.

check.q: Why does the reading say terrorism was hard to respond to?
choices: Because it is a tactic rather than a country, so there was no clear enemy state to defeat
Because the attackers were unknown
Because the military was too small
Because Congress refused to act
check.why: A tactic used by a network cannot be defeated the way a country's army can, which is why the wars had no clear end.

lessons.title: People on the Move
lessons.mainIdea: More people live outside the country of their birth than ever before, and the world's response to migrants and refugees divides nations and neighbors.
reading: Roughly one person in thirty on Earth lives in a country other than the one where he or she was born, about two hundred and eighty million people. Most are *migrants* who moved by choice, for work, study or family. A smaller group are *refugees*: people who fled war or persecution and cannot safely go home. The 1951 Refugee Convention, written after the war had made millions of Europeans homeless, promised that no country would send a refugee back to a place where his or her life was in danger. Most countries signed it. Living up to it has been harder.

The numbers have grown. Syria's civil war, which began in 2011, drove more than half the country's people from their homes; millions crossed into Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan, and in 2015 more than a million reached Europe, many on flimsy boats across the Mediterranean. Wars and hunger in Afghanistan, Sudan, Venezuela and elsewhere added more. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sent millions west within weeks. By the United Nations count, more than one hundred million people were forcibly displaced from their homes in 2022, the most ever recorded. Most refugees are hosted not by rich countries but by poor neighbors of the country they fled.

Migration divides people because it involves real trade-offs. Migrants fill jobs, pay taxes, start businesses and send money home that supports whole villages; economists find that over time they add more to a country than they cost. Yet a sudden arrival can strain schools, housing and hospitals in one town while the benefits spread across the whole economy. Some citizens fear losing jobs or the culture they grew up in. Some governments have built fences and deported people; others have welcomed them. Every wealthy democracy has argued over it, and the arguments have reshaped elections in Europe and the United States.

Chicago has been a city of migrants since it was founded. Poles, Germans, Irish, Italians and Jews in the 1800s; Black families from the South in the Great Migration; Mexicans through the whole twentieth century; and more recently Indians, Chinese, Filipinos and Ukrainians. About one in five Chicagoans was born in another country. In 2022 and 2023 tens of thousands of asylum seekers, mostly from Venezuela, were bused to Chicago from the southern border, and the city struggled to shelter them. The debate you hear in the news is the same one this lesson describes, happening in your own neighborhood.

words.d: a person who moves from one country to another, usually to live and work
a person who has fled his or her country because of war or persecution and cannot safely return
protection granted by a country to a person who has fled danger at home
forced to leave home, whether across a border or within one's own country

look.title: The Refugee Convention's Promise
look.text: The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as a person outside his or her country who has a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, and it forbids sending such a person back to a territory where life or freedom would be threatened.
look.cite: United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, 1951 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Someone fleeing a drought or a collapsed economy does not fit this definition. Should it be widened? What might happen if it were?

check.q: What is the difference between a migrant and a refugee?
choices: Migrants are always poor and refugees are always rich
A migrant moves mostly by choice; a refugee has fled war or persecution and cannot safely go home
Refugees move within their own country only
There is no difference
check.why: The reading distinguishes movement by choice from flight from danger, which the 1951 Convention protects.

check.q: Which countries host most of the world's refugees?
choices: The United States and Canada
Members of the European Union
Australia and Japan
Poor countries next to the country the refugees fled
check.why: Neighbors like Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan took in most Syrians, a pattern true of most refugee flows.

check.q: Why can migration be good for a country as a whole yet still cause conflict?
choices: Because migrants never work
Because benefits spread across the economy while sudden arrivals strain one town's schools and housing
Because migrants refuse to pay taxes
Because all migrants are refugees
check.why: The reading explains that gains are spread thin while costs can land on particular places, and that fears about culture and jobs are real to those who hold them.

lessons.title: Rights Beyond Borders
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1945 the world has written rules that say governments may not do anything they like to their own people, and has struggled to enforce them.
reading: For most of history, what a ruler did inside his own borders was nobody else's business. The Holocaust broke that idea. At Nuremberg in 1945 and 1946, the Allies put Nazi leaders on trial for crimes against humanity and established that following orders was no defense. In December 1948 the United Nations adopted the *Universal Declaration of Human Rights*, drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. It listed rights every person holds simply by being human: life, liberty, fair trials, free speech, free worship, education, and freedom from torture and slavery. It was a statement of principle, not a law, but it gave every movement for rights since a text to point to.

Treaties followed. The 1948 Genocide Convention made the deliberate destruction of a people a crime under international law. The Geneva Conventions of 1949 set rules for war: prisoners must be fed and protected, the wounded cared for, civilians spared. Since then, treaties have banned torture, protected children, and asserted the rights of women. By signing, governments accepted that others could judge them. Whether they lived up to their signatures was another matter. The Cold War superpowers each pointed at the other's abuses and shielded their own allies.

The 1990s tested the system and it mostly failed. In Rwanda in 1994, extremists among the Hutu majority murdered about eight hundred thousand Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about one hundred days, with machetes and radio broadcasts, while UN peacekeepers on the ground were ordered not to intervene and the world argued over the word genocide. In Bosnia in 1995, Serb forces killed about eight thousand Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica, a town the UN had declared a safe area. Afterward, courts were created to try the killers, and in 2002 a permanent *International Criminal Court* opened at The Hague to prosecute genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national courts will not.

The court has convicted a handful of warlords and indicted heads of state. But it has no police force, and the United States, China, Russia and India have not joined it, fearing that their own soldiers or leaders could be charged. Human rights law thus lives in tension: it claims that some acts are crimes everywhere, but it depends on governments to enforce it against themselves. Still, the words matter. A prisoner in a cell, a woman denied school, a worker in a locked factory can all say that the world has agreed their treatment is wrong. In 1900 they could not.

words.d: the 1948 UN statement listing rights that belong to every person
the permanent court at The Hague, opened in 2002, that tries genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity
widespread or systematic attacks on civilians, such as murder, enslavement or torture
soldiers sent by the United Nations to keep or restore peace, usually without authority to fight

look.title: Rights That Belong to Everyone
look.text: The Universal Declaration opens by stating that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, and that everyone is entitled to the rights it lists without distinction of any kind, such as race, color, sex, language, religion, political opinion, national origin, property or birth.
look.cite: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Articles 1 and 2, United Nations, 1948 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: In 1948 several signing countries practiced racial segregation, colonial rule or one-party dictatorship. Why sign a document you are violating? Does the signature still matter?

check.q: What principle did the Nuremberg trials establish?
choices: That only soldiers can be tried for war crimes
That leaders can be tried for crimes against humanity and that following orders is no defense
That the winners of a war may not judge the losers
That genocide is legal in wartime
check.why: Nuremberg held individuals, including top officials, responsible for atrocities regardless of orders.

check.q: What happened in Rwanda in 1994?
choices: UN peacekeepers stopped a planned massacre
The International Criminal Court prevented genocide
About eight hundred thousand people were murdered in about a hundred days while the world failed to act
Rwanda joined the European Union
check.why: The genocide happened with UN troops present but ordered not to intervene, a failure that shaped later reforms.

check.q: What is the main weakness of the International Criminal Court described in the reading?
choices: It has no police and several major powers have not joined it
It cannot try heads of state
It only tries Europeans
It was closed in 2010
check.why: The court depends on governments to arrest suspects, and the United States, China, Russia and India remain outside it.

lessons.title: A Warming Planet
lessons.mainIdea: Burning coal, oil and gas has raised the amount of carbon dioxide in the air and warmed the Earth, and no country can fix it alone.
reading: In 1958 a scientist named Charles Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide in the air on top of a volcano in Hawaii, far from any city. The line he drew has climbed every year since. In 1960 the air held about three hundred and seventeen parts of carbon dioxide per million. By 2020 it held about four hundred and fourteen, higher than at any time in at least eight hundred thousand years, as air bubbles trapped in ancient ice show. The cause is not in doubt: burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon that had been buried for millions of years. *Carbon dioxide* traps heat, as scientists have known since the 1800s. More of it means a warmer planet.

The Earth has warmed about 1.2 degrees Celsius, roughly 2 degrees Fahrenheit, since the late 1800s. That sounds small. It is enough to melt glaciers, raise sea levels, and make heat waves, droughts, wildfires and heavy rains more common. Illinois has seen it: the state's winters have warmed faster than its summers, and the very heavy rains that flood Chicago basements come more often than they did fifty years ago. Farmers in the state plant earlier and face wetter springs. Effects fall hardest on the poor, in Illinois and in the world, because they have the fewest ways to move, rebuild or cool off.

The problem is global in a way that makes it fiendishly hard. Carbon dioxide from a power plant in Ohio or a factory in China mixes into the same air. A country that cuts its own emissions pays the cost while everyone shares the benefit, so each has a reason to wait for the others. Countries that industrialized early, led by the United States, put most of the carbon now in the air there; countries industrializing now, led by China and India, emit the most today and argue that they deserve the same chance to grow. In 2015, in Paris, nearly every country agreed to set its own targets and try to keep warming well below two degrees. The targets so far are not enough to meet that goal.

What to do about it is a political argument, and the evidence bears on it without settling it. Solar and wind power have become the cheapest new electricity in much of the world, and electric cars are spreading, which means cutting emissions costs less than it once did. But coal still powers much of Asia, and oil fuels nearly every ship and plane. People disagree about how fast to change, who should pay, and how much to trust governments to manage it. Those are questions about values as well as facts. The facts, though, are the starting point, and the Keeling curve is still climbing.

words.d: a gas released by burning coal, oil and gas that traps heat in the atmosphere
the long-term warming of the Earth and the shifts in weather patterns that come with it
gases released into the air, especially from burning fuels
the 2015 agreement in which nearly every country set its own targets to limit global warming

look.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air at Mauna Loa
look.unit: parts per million, rounded annual average
look.prompt: By about how much did the number rise in each twenty-year period? Is the rise speeding up, slowing down or steady, and what in the reading would explain that?

check.q: How do scientists know today's carbon dioxide level is higher than at any time in hundreds of thousands of years?
choices: From written records kept by ancient scribes
From air bubbles trapped in ancient ice
From measurements taken by satellites in the 1800s
From the temperature of the ocean
check.why: Ice cores hold tiny samples of ancient air, which let scientists compare past levels with Keeling's measurements.

check.q: Why is climate change so hard for countries to solve, according to the reading?
choices: Because no one knows what causes it
Because it affects only poor countries
Because a country that cuts emissions pays the cost while everyone shares the benefit, so each has reason to wait
Because the Paris Agreement banned solar power
check.why: Shared air means shared benefits from any one country's sacrifice, which tempts every country to let others go first.

check.q: Which statement does the reading present as a matter of values rather than a settled fact?
choices: That carbon dioxide traps heat
That the Earth has warmed about 1.2 degrees Celsius
That the Keeling curve is rising
How fast to change energy systems and who should pay for it
check.why: The physical facts are established; the political choices about speed, cost and trust remain a legitimate argument.

lessons.title: Disease in a Connected World
lessons.mainIdea: Diseases travel as fast as people do, and pandemics from 1918 to COVID-19 show both what global cooperation can do and how easily it fails.
reading: In the fall of 1918, as World War I ended, a new strain of influenza spread along the routes soldiers traveled. It killed about fifty million people worldwide, more than the war itself, most of them young adults. In Chicago, theaters and dance halls were closed and funerals were limited to ten people. There were no vaccines, no antibiotics for the pneumonia that followed, and no way to see the virus, which was too small for the microscopes of the day. Cities that closed schools and gatherings early and kept them closed had fewer deaths, a lesson public health officials remembered a century later.

The twentieth century then won a series of victories. Vaccines defeated polio, which had paralyzed thousands of American children each summer. A worldwide campaign led by the World Health Organization tracked down every case of smallpox, a disease that had killed hundreds of millions, and in 1980 declared it gone from the Earth, the only human disease ever wiped out. Then in 1981 doctors in Los Angeles and New York reported a new illness that destroyed the body's defenses. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has since killed about forty million people, most in Africa. Drugs that keep it in check exist, and the fight to get them to everyone who needs them continues.

In late 2019 a new virus appeared in the Chinese city of Wuhan. By March 2020 it was on every continent, and the World Health Organization declared *COVID-19* a *pandemic*. Air travel had carried it around the world in weeks. Governments closed borders, schools and businesses. Streets in Chicago emptied. Scientists sequenced the virus's genes within days of its discovery and shared them online, and vaccines were developed and tested in under a year, a speed never before achieved. The reported death toll passed seven million; most experts believe the true number is far higher because many deaths were never counted.

The pandemic revealed the connected world at its best and worst. Data flowed freely among scientists, and manufacturers on three continents made billions of vaccine doses. But rich countries bought most of them first, and poor countries waited. Supply chains for masks and medicines snapped. False claims about the virus and the vaccines spread online faster than corrections. Trust in governments and experts fell in many countries. The next lesson turns to the question this raised for everyone: in a world of instant information, how do you decide what to believe?

words.d: a disease outbreak that spreads across many countries or the whole world
the disease caused by a new coronavirus first identified in late 2019
a preparation that trains the body's defenses to fight a disease before infection
the United Nations agency that coordinates the world's response to disease

look.title: Two Cities in 1918
look.text: Philadelphia held a huge parade for the war effort in late September 1918, with two hundred thousand people packed along the streets, even though the flu had already reached the city. St. Louis closed schools, theaters and churches within days of its first cases. In the weeks that followed, Philadelphia's death rate was far higher than St. Louis's.
look.prompt: What does this comparison count as evidence for? What would you need to know to be sure the closures, and not something else, explain the difference?

check.q: What lesson from 1918 did public health officials remember a century later?
choices: That parades stop the spread of disease
That cities that closed gatherings early and kept them closed had fewer deaths
That antibiotics cure influenza
That only old people die of flu
check.why: The comparison of cities in 1918 showed that early, sustained closures saved lives.

check.q: What was unusual about the scientific response to COVID-19?
choices: Scientists refused to share data
No vaccine was ever developed
The virus's genes were shared within days and vaccines were made in under a year
The virus was ignored for a decade
check.why: Rapid sharing of the virus's genetic sequence let researchers worldwide build vaccines at unprecedented speed.

check.q: Which of these is an example of the connected world at its worst during the pandemic?
choices: False claims spreading online faster than corrections, and rich countries buying most vaccines first
Manufacturers on three continents making doses
Scientists sharing data freely
Chicago closing its schools
check.why: The reading contrasts open science with misinformation and unequal access to vaccines.

lessons.title: The Widening Gap
lessons.mainIdea: The world has grown richer and less poor at the same time that wealth within many countries has concentrated at the top, and both trends shape politics.
reading: Two things are true at once. Between countries, the gap has narrowed: China, India and much of Asia have grown far faster than Europe and the United States, so the average person in a poor country is closer to the average person in a rich one than in 1990. Within countries, in many places, the gap has widened. In the United States the share of income going to the top one percent of earners roughly doubled between 1980 and the 2010s, according to standard studies, while the wages of workers without a college degree barely rose after adjusting for prices. A similar story, in different degrees, played out in Britain, China, India and Russia.

Why? Economists point to several causes working together. Technology rewarded people with skills that computers made more valuable and replaced people whose work computers could do. Trade moved factory jobs to lower-wage countries. Unions, which had once pushed wages up for millions, shrank. Tax rates on high incomes fell in many countries after 1980. The rewards for owning things, such as stocks, companies and buildings, grew faster than the rewards for working. Which of these matters most is argued, and the answer differs by country. What is not argued is the pattern.

The gap is visible in Illinois. Chicago's Loop and North Side have some of the highest incomes in the nation, while neighborhoods a few miles south and west have lost factories, stores and population for fifty years. Life expectancy in the wealthiest Chicago neighborhoods runs about thirty years longer than in the poorest, one of the largest such gaps in any American city. Downstate towns that lost a plant to Mexico or to automation have seen young people leave. These are not abstractions to the people living them, and they shape how people vote.

Inequality raises questions that evidence can inform but not settle. Does a large gap slow growth, or does the chance of great wealth drive it? Does it undermine democracy when the rich can fund campaigns and the poor drop out of voting? What should be done: higher taxes on wealth, stronger unions, better schools, a minimum income, or nothing beyond letting markets work? Reasonable people disagree, and every one of these positions has serious economists and voters behind it. A citizen's job is to know the facts, weigh the trade-offs, and decide, rather than accept the first slogan that fits.

words.d: the gap in income or wealth between the richest and poorest people or countries
the replacement of human work by machines or software
an organization of workers that bargains with employers over pay and conditions
what a person owns, such as savings, stocks and property, as distinct from income earned

look.title: Two Miles Apart
look.text: On a summer evening in Chicago, a family in Streeterville eats on a balcony overlooking the lake; their neighborhood has one of the highest life expectancies in the city. A few miles south, in Englewood, a family the same size eats in a house next to a vacant lot where a factory once stood; their neighborhood has one of the lowest. The same city, the same laws, the same year.
look.prompt: List three causes from the reading that might explain the gap between these two neighborhoods. Which of them could a city government change, and which would need national or global action?

check.q: Which statement about inequality since 1990 is supported by the reading?
choices: Gaps between countries and within countries both widened
Gaps between countries and within countries both narrowed
The gap between countries narrowed while gaps within many countries widened
Inequality disappeared in Asia
check.why: Fast growth in Asia narrowed the gap between nations, while within the United States and elsewhere income concentrated at the top.

check.q: Which of these does the reading list as a cause of rising inequality within countries?
choices: The founding of the United Nations
Technology that rewarded some skills and replaced other work, along with trade, weaker unions and lower top tax rates
The end of the Cold War
Rising life expectancy
check.why: Economists point to technology, trade, shrinking unions, falling top taxes and returns on ownership working together.

check.q: How does the reading treat the question of what should be done about inequality?
choices: It says the answer is settled by economists
It says nothing should be done
It says only the rich may decide
It presents several positions with serious support and says citizens must weigh the trade-offs
check.why: The reading frames remedies as a values question informed by evidence, not settled by it.

lessons.title: Where the News Comes From
lessons.mainIdea: Every story you see was chosen, shaped and delivered by someone with reasons, and knowing how news is made is the first step to judging it.
reading: In 1980 most Americans got their news from one of three television networks and a local newspaper, and those outlets decided what counted as news. Today a story reaches you through a feed built by software that chooses what to show you based on what you clicked before. The software, called an *algorithm*, is not trying to inform you. It is trying to keep you watching, because time on the screen is what the company sells to advertisers. Stories that make you angry, afraid or amused keep you watching longer than stories that are merely true and important. That is not a conspiracy. It is a business model, and it shapes what billions of people see every day.

Behind every story is a *source*: the person or record where the information came from. A good reporter names sources, quotes documents and lets you check. A weak story says experts believe or people are saying. Ask who is speaking and how they know. A doctor describing a disease she treats, a government office publishing its own count, and a stranger on a video repeating something a friend told him are not equal, even if the video is more exciting. Ask also who benefits. A story about a miracle cure posted by the company selling it is not the same as one from a hospital.

Every news source has a point of view, and that is not the same as lying. A newspaper owned by a business group, a broadcaster funded by a government, and a site run by an activist will choose different stories and different words for the same event. A refugee crisis in one outlet is a migrant invasion in another. The word bias describes this tilt. The cure is not to find the one unbiased source, which does not exist, but to read across sources with different tilts and notice where they agree. When a right-leaning and a left-leaning outlet report the same facts, those facts are probably solid. Where they differ is where you need to look harder.

The historians' habits taught in this course are the same habits a citizen needs. Who made this? When? Why? What did they leave out? Who else was there, and what would they say? A photograph from a war may be real but from a different war. A quote may be real but cut off before the sentence that changes its meaning. A number may be real but chosen from a range to make one case. None of that is new. What is new is the speed and the volume, and the fact that you, not an editor, are now the one deciding what to pass on.

words.d: a set of computer rules that decides, for example, which stories appear in your feed
the person, document or record from which a piece of information comes
a tilt in how information is chosen and presented, which every source has to some degree
a person who decides which stories are published and checks them before publication

look.title: Three Versions of One Fire
look.text: A factory burns in a small city. Outlet A reports that a fire destroyed a plant and killed two workers, quoting the fire chief. Outlet B reports that lax safety rules killed two workers, quoting a union leader. Outlet C reports that regulations drove the company to cut corners, quoting the owner. A video on social media claims the fire was set on purpose, citing no one.
look.prompt: What do A, B and C agree on? What is each one adding, and who does each source have reason to favor? What should you do with the video?

check.q: What is the goal of the algorithm that builds a social media feed, according to the reading?
choices: To inform users as accurately as possible
To keep users watching so their time can be sold to advertisers
To hide news that the government dislikes
To show every story equally
check.why: The business model rewards attention, which favors stories that provoke strong feelings over stories that are merely important.

check.q: Why does the reading say the cure for bias is not to find one unbiased source?
choices: Because bias is always a lie
Because only government sources are reliable
Because no source is without a point of view, so reading across sources with different tilts works better
Because bias only exists on television
check.why: Every outlet chooses stories and words; comparing sources reveals where the facts hold across different points of view.

check.q: Which of these is the strongest source for a claim about a new disease?
choices: A doctor who treats the disease describing what she sees
A stranger in a video repeating what a friend said
A company selling a cure for it
A post that says experts believe
check.why: The reading ranks sources by how the speaker knows and who benefits; a treating doctor knows firsthand and has no product to sell.

lessons.title: Checking What You See
lessons.mainIdea: A few habits, such as pausing, reading laterally, tracing to the original, and asking what would change your mind, turn a reader into a citizen who is hard to fool.
reading: *Misinformation* is false information spread by people who believe it. *Disinformation* is false information spread on purpose to deceive, often by governments or groups with a goal. Both spread faster than truth: a study of millions of posts found that false stories traveled farther and faster than true ones, mostly because they were more surprising. Governments including Russia's have run operations that create fake accounts posing as ordinary Americans to inflame arguments on both sides of an issue. The goal is not always to make you believe something false. Sometimes it is to make you believe nothing at all.

The first habit is to pause. Strong feeling is the signal to slow down. If a story makes you furious or thrilled, that is exactly when you are easiest to fool, and exactly when a false story is designed to be shared. The second habit is *lateral reading*: instead of studying the page in front of you, open new tabs and find out what other sources say about the site and the claim. Professional fact-checkers do this and outperform professors and students who stay on the page. A site's own About page tells you what it wants you to think of it. Other sites tell you what it is.

The third habit is to trace a claim to its origin. A statistic in a post came from somewhere: a study, a report, a count. Find it. Often the original says something narrower than the post, or says the opposite, or does not exist. A photograph can be checked by searching for the image to see where else it has appeared and when. A quote can be searched to see whether the person said it, and what came before and after. This takes minutes, and it is the difference between knowing and repeating.

The last habit is the hardest. Ask yourself what evidence would change your mind, and go look for it. People are very good at finding reasons to believe what they already believe, and the feed is very good at supplying them. A citizen who cannot name what would change his or her mind is not reasoning but rooting. This course has shown you how historians argue from evidence about slavery, war, revolution and empire. You now live in a world that generates more evidence, and more noise, in a day than those historians saw in a lifetime. The habits are the same. The stakes are yours.

words.d: false information spread by people who think it is true
false information spread deliberately to deceive
checking a source by leaving the page and seeing what other sources say about it
a person whose job is to verify whether claims are true

look.title: The Post That Made You Angry
look.text: A post says that a nearby city has just passed a law that will take something from you, with a screenshot of a headline and thousands of shares. You feel your face get hot. You have your finger on the share button.
look.prompt: Walk through the four habits from the reading in order. What exactly would you do at each step, and what might you find?

check.q: What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
choices: Misinformation is spread on purpose to deceive; disinformation is spread by people who believe it
Misinformation is spread by people who believe it; disinformation is spread on purpose to deceive
Both are always true
Misinformation is only on television
check.why: The reading defines misinformation as honest error and disinformation as deliberate deception.

check.q: What is lateral reading?
choices: Reading a page from left to right
Reading a site's About page carefully
Leaving the page to check what other sources say about the site and the claim
Reading only sources you already trust
check.why: Fact-checkers evaluate a source by looking outside it, which works better than studying the page itself.

check.q: Why does the reading say strong feeling is a signal to slow down?
choices: Because emotions are always wrong
Because true stories never cause strong feelings
Because sharing is illegal when angry
Because false stories are designed to provoke feeling and spread, and that is when a reader is easiest to fool
check.why: Surprise and anger drive sharing, which is exactly what those spreading false stories count on.

review.q: How did the shipping container change the world economy?
choices: It made ships slower but safer
It cut the cost of moving goods so much that products could be made in pieces across many countries
It ended trade between Asia and America
It replaced airplanes
review.why: Cheap, fast container shipping made global supply chains possible.

review.q: Which statement about trade since 1990 does the chapter support?
choices: Everyone gained equally
No one gained
The world as a whole grew richer while losses fell hard on particular places such as factory towns
Only China gained
review.why: Extreme poverty fell worldwide while towns like Galesburg lost their largest employers.

review.q: What bargain has China's Communist Party offered its people since 1978?
choices: Democracy in exchange for taxes
Prosperity in exchange for obedience
Land in exchange for military service
Free speech in exchange for hard work
review.why: Market reforms brought wealth while the party kept its monopoly on power and punished dissent.

review.q: Why did British voters choose to leave the European Union in 2016?
choices: Many felt decisions were being made by people they had not voted for, along with disputes over money and migration
The EU expelled Britain
Britain wanted to adopt the euro
The EU had no members left
review.why: Resentment over sovereignty, the euro crisis and the 2015 refugee arrivals fed the vote to leave.

review.q: What did the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq have in common?
choices: Both found weapons of mass destruction
Both ended within a year
Both were ordered by the United Nations
Both lasted far longer than planned and their results are still debated
review.why: Each war stretched for years, cost thousands of American and far more local lives, and left contested outcomes.

review.q: Which best explains why climate change is hard to solve?
choices: Scientists disagree about whether the Earth is warming
Every country shares the same air, so each is tempted to let others pay the cost of cutting emissions
Carbon dioxide does not trap heat
Only Illinois is affected
review.why: The shared-benefit problem, plus disputes over who put the carbon there, makes cooperation difficult.

review.q: What did the COVID-19 pandemic reveal about the connected world?
choices: That borders no longer matter
That science could move at unprecedented speed while misinformation and unequal access spread just as fast
That vaccines cannot be made quickly
That pandemics only affect poor countries
review.why: Shared data and rapid vaccines showed cooperation at its best; hoarding and false claims showed its failures.

review.q: Which habit does the chapter recommend when a story makes you angry?
choices: Share it quickly before it disappears
Trust it because strong feelings mean it is true
Pause, read laterally, trace the claim to its origin and ask what would change your mind
Report it to the government
review.why: Strong feeling is the signal that a reader is easiest to fool, so the chapter's four habits apply most then.
